page.h1: HTS Chapter 88: Aircraft, Spacecraft, and Parts Thereof — Export Markets & Foreign Tariffs on U.S. Goods

seo.title: Export Markets for U.S. Aircraft & Foreign Tariffs (HTS Ch. 88) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What the EU, China, UK, Brazil and other top markets charge on U.S. aircraft, spacecraft and parts, and who certifies them for sale.
keywords: tariff on US aircraft by country

intro: Who buys U.S. aircraft and parts, and what they charge on it. For almost every market here, the tariff is **0%** — under the WTO Agreement on Trade in Civil Aircraft, a free-trade agreement, or the market's own exemption — so what actually decides access is **airworthiness certification**: whether the buyer's aviation authority (or the FAA, EASA or another authority it recognizes) has certified the specific aircraft or part. China is the one market that still charges a tariff beyond its ordinary rate.
valueBasis: FOB value of U.S. exports, as reported by the United States to UN Comtrade.

profile.headline: U.S. aircraft and parts enter the EU duty-free under the WTO Civil Aircraft Agreement, and the EU has kept its Boeing/Airbus-dispute retaliatory tariffs suspended since 2021 — most recently extended in July 2026 — so none of its authorized countermeasures are in force. EASA type certification (or acceptance of an FAA certificate under the U.S.–EU Bilateral Aviation Safety Agreement) decides whether a specific aircraft or part can be sold here, not the tariff.
profile.mainProducts: Parts of goods of heading 8801, 8802 or 8806 (8807) · Other aircraft (for example, helicopters, airplanes, except unmanned aircraft of heading 8806); spacecraft (including satellites) and suborbital and spacecraft launch vehicles (8802)

regulator.name: European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA)
regulator.requirement: An EASA type certificate (or EASA's validation of an FAA certificate under the U.S.–EU Bilateral Aviation Safety Agreement) for the specific aircraft or part.

profile.headline: China is the only large buyer charging more than it did in January 2025: a 10% extra tariff on all U.S. goods, which reaches finished aircraft and most parts on top of China's already-low ordinary rate. Deliveries of finished Boeing aircraft were paused for several weeks in 2025 amid the tariff dispute and resumed after the May 2025 Geneva truce; CAAC type-validation of the specific aircraft model is the other gate.

markets.name: Mexico
markets.rule: USMCA preferential rate for qualifying U.S.-origin goods

profile.headline: Mexico is not a Civil Aircraft Agreement signatory, but USMCA gives qualifying U.S.-origin aircraft and parts a 0% rate. Qualifying is usually automatic for aircraft built in the U.S., since the product itself is the originating good. AFAC validation of the FAA certificate decides market access.

profile.headline: Singapore keeps tariffs at or near zero on almost everything, aircraft and parts included, and the U.S.–Singapore FTA locks that in for qualifying goods. It is also a major MRO (maintenance, repair and overhaul) hub, which is why parts volumes here are large relative to finished aircraft.

assumptions: Rates reflect each market's treatment of civil aircraft and parts under the WTO Agreement on Trade in Civil Aircraft, a free-trade agreement, or the market's own exemption, applied uniformly across this chapter's six headings for that market; national 8–10-digit lines can still differ by product, so check the cited schedule for the exact line before relying on a number.
The EU is one market: its 27 members share one tariff, and its export figures include every member.

China's extra 10% applies to all U.S.-origin goods, including Chapter 88 aircraft and parts, on top of China's ordinary rate; some imported aviation-maintenance materials may be separately exempt from ordinary duty under China's own 2021 policy — see Tariff updates.

The exportsUsd figures in this matrix are far from complete for most markets and most headings, especially heading 8802 (finished aircraft): official trade statistics redact the value of individual aircraft and large-engine sales for confidentiality, so most cells capture only a small, unrepresentative slice of the real trade. Only the market-level total (this page) and the country-level total (Overview) reconcile with the chapter's real total; read the per-heading cell values as a lower bound, not a true split, and rely on the rate column, not the dollar figures, for what each market charges.
Regulatory requirements are summarised for orientation only; check the regulator's current rules for the specific aircraft or part.
